walkthroughs.body_html:
Computational Thinking — a core area of GCSE Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Computational Thinking brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Computational Thinking.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which technique involves breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems?
options: Abstraction
Decomposition
Iteration
Encapsulation

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of a trace table?
options: To compile code
To track variable values during execution
To draw a flowchart
To store program output

mcqs.q: What is abstraction in computer science?
options: Writing code that does not work.
Removing unnecessary detail to focus on essential features of a problem.
They produce different programming languages.
Making something abstract art or vague.
They produce different programming languages.
The ability of different classes to respond to the same method call in their own way.
Variables that change type at runtime.
Having multiple classes with the same name.

A compiler translates the whole program first; an interpreter executes line by line.
They produce different programming languages.
Writing code that does not work.
